title: The Richest Route and How Many Routes Are Richest

concept.title: Store two numbers in every cell: the best value and the number of ways to get it
body: Coins lie in the cells of a grid. A collector walks from the top left cell to the bottom right cell, moving **right or down**, and takes the coins of every cell on the way (the first and the last cell too). Two things are asked: the **largest** number of coins that can be collected, and **how many different routes** collect exactly that many. Print both numbers; the number of routes is taken modulo 1 000 000 007.

Keep a **pair** for every cell: `best(i, j)`, the most coins on a route ending there, and `ways(i, j)`, the number of routes with that many coins. A route to `(i, j)` came from above or from the left. Compare the two `best` values: if one is larger, only that neighbour can be the previous cell, and `ways` is copied from it; if they are **equal**, both neighbours give optimal routes, and the `ways` are **added**. In both cases `best(i, j)` is the larger value plus the coins of the cell.

body.code:
if up_best > left_best:   best, ways = up_best + coin, up_ways
elif left_best > up_best: best, ways = left_best + coin, left_ways
else:                     best, ways = up_best + coin, (up_ways + left_ways) % MOD

body: This is the standard way to count the *optimal* solutions together with the optimal value: the pair is combined like "maximum with multiplicity". The cells of the first row and the first column have only one neighbour. The time is O(h * w) and the memory O(w) with one row of pairs.

statement: A grid with `h` rows and `w` columns holds `coin(i, j)` coins in each cell. A walk goes from the top left cell to the bottom right cell, moving one cell right or down at a time, and collects the coins of all the visited cells. Print two numbers on one line: the largest number of coins that a walk can collect, and the number of walks that collect that many coins, modulo 1000000007.
inputFormat: The first line has `h` and `w`: the number of rows and columns.
Each of the next `h` lines has `w` numbers: the number of coins in each cell.
outputFormat: Print the largest number of coins and the number of best walks (modulo 1000000007), separated by a space.

examples.note: The best walk 1, 4, 7, 8, 9 collects 29 coins and no other walk collects that many: 29 and 1 walk.
Both walks give 3: the answer is 3 and 2 walks.

hints: Keep, for every cell, the best number of coins and the number of walks that reach it.
If one neighbour has a larger best value, copy its count; if they are equal, add the two counts.
Take the remainder modulo 1000000007 when adding.

h, w = map(int, input().split())
coin = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(h)]

explanation: For every cell the pair (most coins on a walk ending there, number of walks with that many coins) is kept: the larger neighbour value wins and its count is copied, equal values add the counts; the coins of the cell are added to the best value. The pair of the last cell is the answer.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

h, w = map(int, input().split())
coin = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(h)]

MOD = 10 ** 9 + 7
best = [0] * w
ways = [0] * w
for i in range(h):
    row = coin[i]
    for j in range(w):
        v = row[j]
        if i == 0 and j == 0:
            best[0] = v
            ways[0] = 1
            continue
        up_b = best[j] if i > 0 else -1
        up_w = ways[j] if i > 0 else 0
        left_b = best[j - 1] if j > 0 else -1
        left_w = ways[j - 1] if j > 0 else 0
        if up_b > left_b:
            best[j] = up_b + v
            ways[j] = up_w
        elif left_b > up_b:
            best[j] = left_b + v
            ways[j] = left_w
        else:
            best[j] = up_b + v
            ways[j] = (up_w + left_w) % MOD
print(best[w - 1], ways[w - 1])
